name: Akaikos
title: Faithful Messenger from Corinth
summary: Achaicus was a Christian from the church in Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Fortunatus, made the important journey to Ephesus to visit the apostle Paul. They likely delivered a letter from the church and conveyed news about conditions in Corinth. Paul expresses deep gratitude for their visit, writing that they refreshed his spirit, as their personal presence compensated for the distance separating him from the congregation. The apostle urges the Corinthians to show such faithful coworkers respect and recognition. Although Achaicus is mentioned only by name in 1 Corinthians 16:17, his connection to the province of Achaia and his role as a church envoy shed light on the vital network of traveling messengers that linked the early Christian movement across vast geographical distances.

keyEvents.title: Visit to Paul in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: Akaikos traveled with Stephanas and Fortunatus from Corinth to Ephesus to visit the apostle Paul, likely carrying a letter and news from the congregation.

keyEvents.title: Refreshing Encouragement for Paul
keyEvents.description: Akaikos and his fellow travelers refreshed Paul's spirit by their visit and compensated with their personal presence for the distance that separated the apostle from the congregation in Corinth.

keyEvents.title: Recognition from Paul
keyEvents.description: Paul urged the Corinthians to recognize such co-workers and to submit themselves to those who have devoted themselves to serving the holy ones.

versions.summary: Achaicus was a Christian from Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Fortunatus, visited the apostle Paul in Ephesus. He brought news from the church in Corinth and helped to refresh Paul's spirit. He is mentioned only in 1 Corinthians and is regarded as a faithful servant in the early church.

versions.reason: [minor] The title is good but could be expanded slightly to mention the connection to Paul more explicitly, e.g., 'Faithful Messenger from Corinth to Paul'. The current wording is nevertheless acceptable.; [minor] The role 'disciple' is general. 'Messenger' or 'church servant' would have been more precise for Stephanas's function as described in 1 Cor 16:17-18.; [minor] That Achaicus was part of Stephanas's household is a common speculation, but it is not explicitly confirmed in the text. The description correctly says 'probably', but it should be clarified that this is an interpretation, not direct biblical information.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include at least some notes on the origin of the name (Greek Ἀχαϊκός, meaning 'from Achaia'), the historical context for the journey between Corinth and Ephesus, and possibly Achaicus's potential status as a slave or freed person based on naming traditions.

versions.summary: Achaicus was a Christian from Corinth who, together with Stephanas and Fortunatus, visited the apostle Paul in Ephesus. They brought news and likely a letter from the church in Corinth, and refreshed Paul's spirit through their presence and service. Paul encouraged the church to recognize such men for their devotion. Achaicus is mentioned only in 1 Corinthians 16:17 and is regarded as a faithful servant and messenger in the early church.

versions.reason: [minor] The third key event regarding 'Recognition from Paul' should also include verse 18 in its entirety, but the actual call for recognition is strictly found in verse 18. The reference is correct, but verse 16 is also relevant since Paul there urges submission to such fellow workers. Consider including verses 15–16 for completeness.; [minor] 1 Cor 16:15–16 contains Paul's direct appeal to submit to the household of Stephanas and all who work and strive with them. Verse 18b ('Show respect/recognition to such people') connects directly. Including verses 15–16 in addition to verse 18 could strengthen the reference.; [minor] The footnote's mention that they 'possibly also brought back 1 Corinthians as a reply' is a reasonable but speculative assumption. It is a traditional interpretation, but it is worth noting that this is not explicitly confirmed in the text. The wording is acceptable as it stands, though it could have been more cautious.

They likely delivered a letter from the congregation and brought news about conditions in Corinth. Paul expresses gratitude for their visit, writing that they refreshed his spirit and made up for what the congregation could not contribute through its absence. The apostle urges the Corinthians to show such faithful coworkers recognition and respect. Achaicus is mentioned only in 1 Corinthians 16:17, but the connection of his name to the province of Achaia and his role as a church envoy testify to the important network of messengers that held the early Christian movement together across geographical distances.

versions.reason: [minor] Verses 15–16 in 1 Corinthians 16 deal primarily with the household of Stephanas and the call to submit to such fellow workers. Verses 15 and 16 do not mention Achaicus directly, although the context is relevant. It may be considered to limit the reference to verses 16 and 18, which are more directly connected to the appeal for recognition.; [minor] The phrasing "replaced what the congregation could not contribute itself through its absence" is somewhat unclear—it can be understood as referring to Achaicus's absence. It should be clarified that it is the congregation's absence from Paul that is meant.

footnotes.text: The name Achaicus (Greek: Ἀχαϊκός, Achaïkos) means 'from Achaia' and refers to the Roman province of Achaia in southern Greece, where Corinth was the capital. The name was common among slaves and freedmen in Roman times and may indicate that Achaicus originally had a lower social status.

The journey from Corinth to Ephesus, where Paul was staying, likely went by sea across the Aegean Sea. This route was well organized in Roman times and widely used for trade and communication between the two important port cities. The distance was approximately 400 km by sea.

That Paul mentions Achaicus, Stephanas, and Fortunatus by name in 1 Cor 16:17 suggests that they had an important role as intermediaries between the apostle and the church in Corinth. They may have delivered the church's letter to Paul (cf. 1 Cor 7:1) and possibly also brought back 1 Corinthians as a response.

In the early church, such messengers (Greek: apostoloi ekklesion, 'church envoys') served as important links between the churches and the apostles. They ensured the flow of information, delivery of gifts, and maintenance of fellowship across geographical distances.

Some scholars have linked Achaicus to Stephanas' household (1 Cor 1:16; 16:15), since both were from Corinth and appeared together. If Achaicus belonged to Stephanas' household, this could further support the assumption that he was a freed slave or servant, which was common in the Pauline churches.

The phrase 'refreshed my spirit' (Greek: anepausan to emon pneuma) used by Paul in 1 Cor 16:18 is also found in Philemon 1:7 and 1:20, and refers to the deep emotional and spiritual encouragement that personal fellowship and service could provide in the early Christian movement.
